passage.text_en:
Coral reefs are among the most biologically diverse ecosystems on Earth, supporting roughly a quarter of all marine species despite covering less than one percent of the ocean floor. The vibrant colors of healthy coral come not from the coral itself but from microscopic algae called zooxanthellae that live within coral tissues. These algae provide coral with most of its nutrients through photosynthesis, while the coral provides shelter and essential compounds in return.

When ocean temperatures rise even slightly above normal, this delicate partnership breaks down. The coral expels the algae, losing both its color and its main food source. This process, known as coral bleaching, leaves the coral white and weakened. If conditions return to normal quickly, the algae may return and the coral can recover. However, if elevated temperatures persist, the coral starves and eventually dies.

Climate change has dramatically increased the frequency and severity of bleaching events. The Great Barrier Reef, for instance, has experienced mass bleaching multiple times within just one decade — an unprecedented rate that scientists warn the reef cannot sustain. Some researchers are now developing 'heat-resistant' coral strains in laboratories, while others focus on reducing local stressors such as pollution and overfishing. Although these efforts may help, most experts agree that the long-term survival of coral reefs depends on global action to slow ocean warming.
